## Learning goals

::: {.nonincremental}
- **Choose** a review type that fits the purpose
- **Explain** what a review can and cannot establish
- **Translate** a topic into a concept table and a search string
- **Assess** a search: precision, recall, validation
- **Select** studies by explicit criteria; document in a **PRISMA** flow diagram
- **Synthesise** with a concept matrix, not by summarising
- **Identify** biases — in literature, databases, search and synthesis
- **Use** AI at each stage without losing reproducibility
:::

## How this lecture works

::: {.dek}
Nine chapters · one self-check each · a tutorial step for every chapter
:::

- **Reference model:** the *systematic* literature review

- **Payoff:** the review section of your term paper or thesis

- **Pause tasks:** stop the video, do the task

- **Take-home II:** same steps — watch all chapters first

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Rarely a systematic review — always a review section
:::

::: {.notes}
Most of you will never publish a stand-alone systematic review, but every
term paper and thesis has a literature review section. The systematic review
is the reference model because its standards make every review section
better. The tutorial on the lecture page turns each chapter into a step you
carry out yourself, and the take-home examination follows the same steps.
:::

## One literature runs through all chapters

::: {.dek}
Capabilities and routines — evolutionary economics meets business studies
:::

- **Routines:** the "genes" of the firm [@nelson1982evolutionary]

- **Absorptive capacity:** recognise, assimilate, apply external knowledge [@cohen1990absorptive]

- **Dynamic capabilities:** integrate, build, reconfigure competences [@teece1997dynamic]

- **Routine dynamics:** routines as a source of change [@feldman2003reconceptualizing]

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Running question: "How do empirical studies conceptualise and measure
capabilities and routines when explaining firm-level innovation?"
:::

::: {.notes}
This literature sits at the intersection of evolutionary economics and
business studies, and different communities describe overlapping ideas with
different words. That makes it a good example for almost every problem in
this lecture: choosing a review type, building a search string, synthesising
inconsistent concepts, and terminology bias.
:::

## What a review is for {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
01
:::

## A review is a study whose data are other studies

::: {.dek}
Question · method · checkable result
:::

- **Map** a field — actors, concepts, methods

- **Establish** what is known, and how robustly

- **Find** gaps and contradictions

- **Build** or refine a framework

- **Justify** a research question

::: {.keybox .fragment}
No question, no review
:::

::: {.notes}
What separates a review from reading around a topic is that it has a
question, a method, and a result someone else could check. If you cannot
state your question, you are not reviewing yet.
:::

## Review as a method ≠ review as a section

::: {.dek}
Same logic, different scale
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Stand-alone review
:::

- Review **is** the contribution

- Full protocol, several databases, two screeners

- Full **PRISMA** report

- e.g. @schilke2018quo
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Review section
:::

- Review **motivates** the contribution

- One database, documented string, explicit criteria

- One **paragraph** + flow diagram

- Paper, thesis, report
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Discipline of the left · scale of the right
:::

## Choose the review type by purpose

::: {.dek}
Purpose first, label second
:::

| Type | Purpose | Search | Synthesis | Example |
|:-----|:--------|:-------|:----------|:--------|
| Narrative | Overview, interpretation | Selective, often undocumented | Narrative | Textbook chapters |
| Integrative | New framework from diverse work | Purposive, documented | Conceptual | @becker2004organizational |
| Scoping | Size and variety of a field | Broad, documented | Mapping, counts | @arksey2005scoping (method) |
| Systematic | Focused question | Exhaustive, reproducible | Structured, often thematic | @lane2006reification |
| Meta-analysis | Pooled effect sizes | Exhaustive | Statistical | @orlitzky2003corporate |
| Bibliometric | Structure of a field | Database export | Citation networks | — |

: {.tasks}

::: {.source}
Simplified from @snyder2019literature and @grant2009typology. Lane et al.:
289 papers from 14 journals.
:::

::: {.notes}
Real reviews mix types. The label matters less than being explicit about
what you did. Becker reviews the routines literature since Nelson and Winter;
Orlitzky et al. pool studies on corporate social and financial performance.
:::

## One literature, several review types

::: {.dek}
Capabilities: what each type delivers on the same subject
:::

- **Integrative:** routines literature "riddled with ambiguities"
  [@becker2004organizational]

- **Critical systematic:** absorptive capacity *reified* — widely used,
  rarely examined [@lane2006reification]

- **Content-analytic:** meta-framework of dynamic capabilities
  [@schilke2018quo]

- **Meta-analysis:** not meaningful — measures too different to pool

::: {.keybox .fragment}
State of the literature → possible review type
:::

## What a review can do

::: {.dek}
Legitimate claims of a good review
:::

- **Map** a debate and its positions

- **Establish** how much evidence exists, and of which kind

- **Show** agreement, conflict, context dependence

- **Locate** gaps — relative to a documented search

- **Clarify** inconsistently used concepts

## What a review cannot do

::: {.dek}
Limits of every review — however careful
:::

- **Better evidence** than its primary studies

- **Proof of absence** — only "not found by this search"

- **Objectivity** through method — every step a choice

- **Causal answers** the primary studies lack

- **Evidence** from the frequency of a claim

::: {.keybox .fragment}
No substitute for reading the key works
:::

::: {.notes}
These limits hold however carefully you work, and naming them is a sign of
competence, not weakness. A review cannot produce better evidence than the
studies it rests on. It cannot prove that something has not been studied,
only that your documented search did not find it. Being systematic does not
make it objective: question, database, terms and criteria are all choices.
:::

## Spotlight: QWERTY — mapped, not settled

::: {.dek}
Path dependence · contested for decades
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Lock-in
:::

- Technical interrelatedness, scale economies, quasi-irreversibility
  [@david1985clio]

- → markets can lock in **inferior** standards
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
"Fable of the keys"
:::

- Weak evidence for Dvorak's superiority, partly from Dvorak himself
  [@liebowitz1990fable]

- → lock-in claim **not established**
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Review: which evidence each side rests on · primary research: who types faster
:::

::: {.taskbox .nonincremental}
Claim: "My systematic review shows there is no research on dynamic
capabilities in family firms."

- Two reasons for scepticism?
- A defensible rewording?
:::

## Workflow and question {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
02
:::

## Six stages — the first before any search

::: {.dek}
Each stage constrains the next · question changed after the results ≈ p-hacking
:::

::: {.grid2}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[1 Protocol · 2 Search]{.caphead}

Question, scope, criteria **in writing** · then a documented search
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[3 Screening · 4 Extraction]{.caphead}

Criteria on titles, abstracts, full texts · fixed extraction format
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[5 Synthesis]{.caphead}

By concept, not by author · explain agreement and disagreement
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[6 Reporting]{.caphead}

What you did, what you found, what your choices cost
:::
:::

::: {.source}
After @tranfield2003towards: the medical template adapted to management
research.
:::

## A topic is not a question

::: {.dek}
Reviewable: object · context · what you want to know
:::

- **Too broad:** "What do we know about capabilities?"

- **Too narrow:** "Does absorptive capacity raise patenting in German
  biotech SMEs in 2015?"

- **Reviewable:** "How do empirical studies conceptualise and measure
  capabilities and routines when explaining firm-level innovation?"

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Test: two people, same in/out decisions?
:::

## The concept table: building blocks of the search

::: {.dek}
One column per concept · one row per wording
:::

| Capabilities & routines | Innovation | Empirical measurement |
|:------------------------|:-----------|:----------------------|
| dynamic capabilities | innovation, innovative | measurement, measure |
| organizational / organisational routines | "new product" | operationalization / operationalisation |
| absorptive capacity | patent | empirical |
| organizational / organisational capabilities | R&D | survey |
| technological capabilities | | "panel data" |
| competences, competencies | | |

::: {.source}
Spelling variants listed explicitly · plural forms covered by stemming ·
third column: in the string or in the criteria — document the choice
:::

## Criteria: fixed before the results

::: {.dek}
Part of the protocol · replicable by a second person
:::

- **Content:** capability or routine construct, related to innovation

- **Design:** empirical, quantitative or qualitative; conceptual papers out

- **Type:** peer-reviewed articles, reviews; book chapters out — with reason

- **Period, language:** e.g. 1990 onwards, English → **reported limitation**

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Contestable is fine — invisible is not
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 2 {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox .nonincremental}
Your own topic:

- A reviewable question
- A concept table: ≥ 2 concepts, ≥ 4 terms each
- Keep it — needed for the tutorial
:::

## Searching {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
03
:::

## Not every search system fits a systematic review

::: {.dek}
Requirements: reliable search · precise query · documented, rerunnable
:::

- **OpenAlex:** free, open, broad coverage, Boolean, scriptable
  [@priem2022openalex]

- **Web of Science, Scopus:** curated, precise syntax — paid, access fragile

- **Google Scholar:** huge coverage — limited Boolean control, ranked, not
  reproducible

- Only **14 of 28** systems fit for systematic reviews [@gusenbauer2020which]

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Baseline: OpenAlex · paid databases: optional add-on
:::

::: {.notes}
The baseline taught here does not depend on any subscription. OpenAlex is
free, open and the same for everyone, so every search in this lecture can be
rerun by anyone. Web of Science and Scopus remain useful where you have
access — mainly for their precise search syntax and curated metadata — but
access through a university is fragile and ends with graduation. Google
Scholar is fine for finding a paper you already know exists, but not as the
search of a systematic review.
:::

## Three families of search tools

::: {.dek}
Different logics → different roles in a review
:::

::: {.grid2}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[Keyword (Boolean) search]{.caphead}

Matches your terms · transparent, reproducible · blind to unknown words
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Semantic (AI) search]{.caphead}

Matches meaning · reveals vocabulary · opaque, not reproducible
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Citation-based search]{.caphead}

Follows seed papers' citations · finds what keywords miss — within one community
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[In a review]{.caphead}

Boolean: **backbone** · semantic: **input** to the concept table · citation:
**supplement**
:::
:::

## From concept table to search string

::: {.dek}
OR within a concept · AND between concepts · searched in title and abstract
:::

```text
("dynamic capabilities" OR "organizational routines" OR "organisational routines"
 OR "absorptive capacity" OR "organizational capabilities"
 OR "organisational capabilities" OR "technological capabilities")
AND (innovation OR innovative OR "new product" OR patent)
AND (measurement OR measure OR empirical OR survey)
```

- **Operators:** AND, OR, NOT — in capitals

- **Quotation marks:** phrases

- **Stemming:** plurals automatic — derivations and spellings listed

- **Filters:** years, type, language — documented separately

::: {.source}
OpenAlex syntax, field `title_and_abstract.search`. No wildcards in the web
interface. Current rules: OpenAlex help pages and tutorial.
:::

## Every search trades recall against precision

::: {.dek}
Both maximised: impossible · systematic reviews: recall first
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Recall (sensitivity)
:::

- Share of all **relevant** papers found

- Low → review **incomplete**, unnoticed
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Precision
:::

- Share of **found** papers that are relevant

- Low → **thousands** of irrelevant titles to screen
:::
:::

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Wider string: recall ↑ precision ↓ · narrower: the reverse
:::

## Recall: tested against known papers

::: {.dek}
All relevant papers: unknown · some: known · missed known → missed unknown
:::

- Before searching: **5–10 key papers** that must appear

- Incl. **closed-access** papers from large publishers (next slide)

- Run the string → how many retrieved?

- **Missed one?** Its title and keywords → the missing term

- Revise, rerun, **log every version**

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Illustrative: v1 finds 5/8 → + "competenc\*", "routine\*" → v2 finds 8/8
:::

## The blind spot: records without abstract

::: {.dek}
No abstract → title and keywords only · gap not random
:::

- ~**40%** of OpenAlex records without abstract [@borrego2025openalex]

- Concentrated: **closed-access** Elsevier and Springer Nature articles — core
  outlets in business and economics [@kramer2024open]

- Consequence: **recall loss** for exactly these papers

- Adding abstracts later: helps **screening**, not **search**

::: {.notes}
OpenAlex searches titles and abstracts. For a record without an abstract,
only the title and OpenAlex's keywords can match. The gap is systematic:
closed-access articles of the largest publishers lost their abstracts after
takedown requests. You can always look up the abstract on the publisher's
page when screening, but a record your string never retrieved will not be
screened at all. Chapter 6 returns to why this happens.
:::

## Countermeasures: what the method can compensate

::: {.dek}
Baseline workflow · no paid tools needed
:::

- **Snowballing: compulsory** — citation links independent of abstracts

- **Test set** with closed-access papers → gap visible

- **Title terms:** words authors put in titles

- **Measure** the gap: share of hits without abstract, by publisher and year

- **Report** it as a limitation

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Optional add-on: same string in a paid database — compare hit lists
:::

## Spotlight: words follow communities

::: {.dek}
Capabilities: overlapping ideas, different names
:::

- **Evolutionary economics:** routines, organisational capabilities
  [@nelson1982evolutionary]

- **Strategic management:** dynamic capabilities, resources, core competences
  [@teece1997dynamic]

- **Organisation studies:** routine dynamics [@feldman2003reconceptualizing]

- **Innovation and development studies:** technological capabilities,
  absorptive capacity [@cohen1990absorptive]

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Only "dynamic capabilit\*" → one community's view as "the field"
:::

## Snowballing: what keywords missed

::: {.dek}
From a few strong included papers · both directions [@wohlin2014guidelines]
:::

- **Backward:** reference lists of the seed papers

- **Forward:** papers citing the seeds (OpenAlex: *Cited by*)

- **Same criteria** as for database results

- **Separate box** in the flow diagram

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Supplement, never substitute — with OpenAlex: compulsory
:::

## Screening and selection {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
04
:::

## Screening in two rounds

::: {.dek}
Cheap decisions first · protocol criteria only
:::

- **Round 1 — titles, abstracts:** clearly out → exclude; in doubt → keep

- **No abstract?** Publisher page via DOI — abstracts free to read there

- **Round 2 — full texts:** decide; **reason** for every exclusion

- **Second screener:** all records, or a sample; disagreements resolved

- **Criteria drift:** criterion changed → restart, document

::: {.arrow .fragment}
One row per record + reason column → template in the tutorial
:::

## The flow diagram: the fate of every record

::: {.dek}
Illustrative numbers · mandatory in a systematic review
:::

| Stage | What is counted | n |
|:------|:----------------|--:|
| Identification | Records from the database | 612 |
| Screening | Excluded on title / abstract | 540 |
| | Full texts sought / not retrievable | 72 / 3 |
| Eligibility | Full texts assessed / excluded with reasons | 69 / 41 |
| | *Not empirical (15), no innovation outcome (18), other (8)* | |
| Other sources | Added through snowballing | 6 |
| Included | Studies in the synthesis | 34 |

::: {.source}
Template: @page2021prisma. R package PRISMA2020 [@haddaway2022prisma2020]
→ tutorial.
:::

::: {.notes}
The flow diagram is also the easiest way to make the review section of a
paper checkable: a reader sees immediately how many records you started
with and why studies dropped out.
:::

## Check yourself — chapter 4 {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox .nonincremental}
- Reasons for every full-text exclusion — but not for title/abstract
  exclusions: why?
- What can a reader do with them?
:::

## From summary to synthesis {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
05
:::

## Weak reviews: a list of summaries

::: {.dek}
Same sources · organised by author vs. by idea
:::

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Author-centric
:::

- "Nelson and Winter (1982) describe … Teece et al. (1997) define …
  Feldman and Pentland (2003) argue …"

- Reader: **so what?**
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
Concept-centric
:::

- "The literature disagrees on whether routines stabilise or change firms …"

- Stability (Nelson & Winter) vs. change from within (Feldman & Pentland)

- The disagreement **is** the finding
:::
:::

::: {.notes}
A concept-centric paragraph could read: The literature disagrees on whether
routines stabilise or change firms. Early evolutionary work stresses
stability; later work locates change inside routines. Dynamic capabilities
can be read as an attempt to bridge both. The paragraph is organised around
the disagreement, and the sources are evidence for positions in it.
:::

## The concept matrix forces synthesis

::: {.dek}
Rows: studies · columns: concepts · simplified [@webster2002analyzing]
:::

| Study | Construct | Level | Main emphasis | Evidence |
|:------|:----------|:------|:--------------|:---------|
| @nelson1982evolutionary | Routines | Firm | Stability, heredity | Theory, simulation |
| @cohen1990absorptive | Absorptive capacity | Firm | Cumulative learning from prior knowledge | Theory, R&D-based empirics |
| @teece1997dynamic | Dynamic capabilities | Firm | Reconfiguration for change | Conceptual |
| @feldman2003reconceptualizing | Routine dynamics | Routine | Change from within routines | Conceptual, field-based |

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Read by column → synthesis
:::

## Data extraction fills the matrix

::: {.dek}
Columns fixed before reading · piloted on three papers
:::

- **Bibliographic:** authors, year, outlet

- **Design:** sample, country, period, method

- **Constructs:** definition and **measurement**

- **Findings:** direction, size, conditions

- **Quality:** reasons for more or less trust

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Tempting for AI — silent errors across the sample (ch. 7)
:::

## Spotlight: firm growth — conflicting results, sorted

::: {.dek}
Gibrat's law: growth independent of size · no single answer · structured disagreement
:::

- Results depend on the **sample**: all firms, survivors, or above minimum
  size [@mansfield1962entry]

- … and on **sector, size class, country, period** [@santarelli2006gibrat]

- Vote count (say, "12 for, 15 against"): **uninformative**

- Matrix by sample and method: **when** the law holds

::: {.source}
Book-length synthesis: @coad2009growth.
:::

## Spotlight: same concept, different measures

::: {.dek}
Related variety: related industries in a region · evolutionary economic geography
:::

- Origin: an **entropy-based** measure [@frenken2007related]

- Review of **21** studies: mostly positive for employment growth; partly only
  knowledge-intensive sectors [@content2016related]

- Different **measures** and **levels** of relatedness

- Synthesis question: *same concept, or same word?*

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Pooling different measures: precise answer, no question
:::

## Quality appraisal: unequal weight

::: {.dek}
Medical tools fit management only partly · short explicit questions beat none
:::

- **Construct:** clearly defined, consistently measured?

- **Design:** able to support the claim?

- **Sample:** described — who is missing?

- **Limitations:** acknowledged by the authors?

## Check yourself — chapter 5 {.no-dash}

::: {.taskbox .nonincremental}
The review section of a paper you recently read:

- Author- or concept-centric?
- Sketch the concept matrix it should have used
:::

## Biases, limitations, caveats {.divider background-color="#00395B"}

::: {.secnum}
06
:::

## Bias at every stage

::: {.dek}
Inherited from the literature → report · introduced by you → reduce
:::

::: {.grid2}
::: {.cap .fragment}
[The literature]{.caphead}

Publication bias · citation bias · survivorship in primary samples
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Database and search]{.caphead}

Coverage bias · terminology bias · ranking and tool effects
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Screening]{.caphead}

Confirmation bias · single-screener judgement · criteria drift
:::

::: {.cap .fragment}
[Synthesis and reporting]{.caphead}

Vote counting · apples and oranges · overclaiming from absence
:::
:::

## Publication bias: a filtered literature

::: {.dek}
Significant, novel, positive → more likely published · reviews inherit the filter
:::

- 159 empirical economics literatures: ~**80%** of effects exaggerated,
  typically **× 2** [@ioannidis2017power]

- CSR and profitability, 512 studies: **small** positive effect,
  **publication bias** [@hirsch2023csr]

- vs. an earlier meta-analysis: clearly positive link [@orlitzky2003corporate]

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Counting published results = measuring the publication process, too
:::

## Citation bias: often cited ≠ well supported

::: {.dek}
Citations attract citations · works cited for what they are believed to say
:::

- Absorptive capacity, 289 papers: construct **reified** — used as given,
  rarely examined [@lane2006reification]

- Citation-based tools: **amplify** — they find what is already cited

- AI summaries: **amplify** again — the dominant reading

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Read the original · check how it is used
:::

## Survivorship bias: inherited from primary studies

::: {.dek}
Aggregation can hide it
:::

- Survivors-only growth samples: exited small firms missing → small firms
  look faster-growing (cf. @mansfield1962entry)

- Capability building: failed attempts rarely observed

- **Code** the sample design — or the bias is averaged in

## Coverage bias: the database decides

::: {.dek}
Curation = selection · selection ≠ neutral
:::

- Web of Science, Scopus: natural sciences and **English** over-, **social
  sciences** and humanities under-represented [@mongeon2016journal]

- **Books, working papers, Global South:** weak in curated databases

- OpenAlex: broader, less English-centred — but **metadata gaps**: abstracts,
  language tags [@cespedes2025linguistic]

::: {.arrow .fragment}
No neutral database · test with known papers, report the gaps
:::

## Terminology bias: the pluralism problem of search

::: {.dek}
Search terms encode a perspective
:::

- "Dynamic capabilities" ≠ "routines" ≠ "technological capabilities" — yet
  overlapping

- Heterodox vs. mainstream: different **names**, same phenomenon

- Result: **systematic**, yet **one-sided**

- **Countermeasures:** terms from several communities, alternative strings,
  compared hit lists

## Political economy: who owns the record of science?

::: {.dek}
What you can find depends on who controls publications and metadata
:::

- Five publishers: **> 50%** of all papers by 2013 [@lariviere2015oligopoly]

- Owners of the indexes: **Elsevier** → Scopus · **Clarivate** → Web of Science

- Abstracts withdrawn from open indexes: Springer Nature 2022, Elsevier 2024
  — abstracts as **assets**, e.g. for AI licensing [@kramer2024open]

- Counter-movement: **open research information** — Barcelona Declaration
  2024; Sorbonne and CNRS leave commercial databases [@barcelona2024declaration]

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Missing abstracts: a political decision, not a technical accident
:::

::: {.notes}
The missing abstracts from chapter 3 are not a technical glitch. A handful
of commercial publishers control a large share of the scholarly record, and
the two dominant curated indexes are themselves commercial products — Scopus
belongs to Elsevier, a publisher. Abstracts are publicly readable on
publisher pages, but publishers have withdrawn the right to redistribute
them in open indexes, at a time when abstracts have become valuable, among
other things, for training and licensing AI systems. Universities are
responding: the Barcelona Declaration of 2024 commits signatories to open
research information; Sorbonne University dropped Web of Science in favour
of OpenAlex in 2024, and the CNRS left Scopus in 2024 and Web of Science in
2026. Choosing a database is therefore also choosing an infrastructure.
:::

## Reviewer bias: screening and synthesis

::: {.dek}
Reviewer = part of the instrument · protocol = constraint
:::

- **Confirmation bias:** fitting borderline papers stay in

- **Criteria drift:** criteria change while reading

- **Vote counting:** significant results counted, evidence not weighed

- **Apples and oranges:** different constructs and designs pooled

- **Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence**

::: {.keybox .fragment}
Fixed criteria · second screener · concept matrix · careful wording
:::

## AI: helpful at some stages, risky at others

::: {.dek}
AI suggests · the documented, reproducible step is yours
:::

| Stage | AI can help with | Typical failure | Rule |
|:------|:-----------------|:----------------|:-----|
| Question, concept table | Synonyms, neighbouring vocabularies | Converges on dominant terms | Check terms against key papers |
| Search | Papers you missed | Opaque, non-reproducible | Never the primary search |
| Screening | First sort of titles | Plausible but wrong exclusions | You decide; log reasons |
| Extraction | Reading many PDFs | Silent errors across the sample | Verify a sample by hand |
| Synthesis, writing | Structure, critique of drafts | Generic, mainstream synthesis | Your matrix, your argument |

::: {.arrow .fragment}
Disclose every use
:::

::: {.secnum}

## What to take away

- A review = a **study**: question, method, checkable result

- **Open baseline:** concept table → OpenAlex string → test → snowball → log

- **Synthesis** by concept — via the concept matrix

- Bias at **every** stage, incl. database ownership: reduce, then report

- AI **suggests** — the documented step is **yours**

::: {.keybox .lg .fragment}
Systematic ≠ objective — choices made visible
:::

## Can and cannot, once more

::: {.columns .divided}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
A review can
:::

- Map a debate — QWERTY, routines, Gibrat

- Show context dependence

- Locate gaps relative to a documented search
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.colhead}
A review cannot
:::

- Exceed its primary studies

- Prove absence

- Turn frequency into evidence
:::
:::
